title: North America
description: How California, Oregon, Washington and Canada built their own wine cultures in under a century.
L: An American Viticultural Area, or AVA, is a defined grape-growing area with distinct geography. There are over 270. AVAs set boundaries only, not grapes, yields or methods. They can nest: Oakville sits inside Napa Valley, which sits inside the larger North Coast AVA.

A wine naming an AVA needs at least 85% of grapes from it. A varietal name needs 75% of that grape, though Oregon requires 90% for most varieties. A vintage needs 95% from that year when an AVA is named. A state name, like California, needs 100% from that state.
An AVA only defines where the grapes grow. Producers choose grapes and methods freely.

From 1920 to 1933, Prohibition banned the sale of alcohol in the US. Most wineries closed, vineyards were replanted with table grapes or thick-skinned varieties for home winemaking. The industry restarted slowly. Modern fine wine in California really grew from the 1960s, with Robert Mondavi founding his Napa winery in 1966.
In Oregon, a wine labelled Pinot Noir must contain at least 90% of that grape.
Yes. Oregon sets a stricter rule than the federal 75% for most varieties.
An AVA defines a place, not grapes or methods
Labels need 85% from an AVA and 75% of a named grape
Prohibition set American wine back by decades
Describe Napa Valley's climate and sub-AVAs

Napa Valley, north of San Francisco, is about 50 km long. Cool air and fog come in from San Pablo Bay in the south, so the south, Carneros, is cool, and the north, Calistoga, is hot. Cabernet Sauvignon is the star. Sub-AVAs include Oakville, Rutherford and Stags Leap District on the valley floor, and Howell Mountain and Spring Mountain in the hills.

The cold California Current chills the Pacific. As inland valleys heat up, they draw cool, damp air and fog in through gaps in the coastal hills. Fog keeps mornings cool and preserves acidity; it burns off later, letting the sun ripen grapes. It explains why North Coast wines can be ripe yet balanced.
Why is Carneros cooler than Calistoga?
Closer to the cool bay and fog
Carneros, at the southern end, gets more cool air and fog from San Pablo Bay.

Sonoma, west of Napa, is larger and more varied. The Russian River Valley and Sonoma Coast, cooled by fog, make Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Dry Creek Valley and Alexander Valley, warmer, make Zinfandel and Cabernet. Old-vine Zinfandel is a Sonoma speciality.
Cool coast to warm inland valleys
Match each AVA to its signature grape.
Each part of the North Coast has its own climate and grape.
Napa runs from cool Carneros to hot Calistoga, with Cabernet the star
Pacific fog keeps North Coast wines fresh
Sonoma ranges from cool Pinot Noir to warm Zinfandel
Explain the transverse valleys of Santa Barbara

The Central Coast runs from San Francisco Bay to Santa Barbara. Monterey's Salinas Valley is cool and windy, good for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Paso Robles is warmer, with large day and night swings, making Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Rhône grapes, a movement known as the Rhône Rangers.

In Santa Barbara County, the Santa Ynez Valley runs east to west, unusual on the American coast. This lets cold Pacific air flow straight in. The Sta. Rita Hills, near the sea, are cool enough for fine Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; further inland, Happy Canyon is warm enough for Bordeaux grapes.
East-west valleys bring in the ocean
Santa Barbara's valleys run east to west, letting ocean air flow inland.
Yes. That orientation brings cool Pacific air deep into the valleys, making them ideal for Pinot Noir.
The film Sideways, set in Santa Barbara County in 2004, made Pinot Noir sales jump in the US, and hurt Merlot's reputation for years.
Which grapes are associated with the Rhône Rangers in Paso Robles?
Rhône Rangers grow Rhône grapes like Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Viognier.
The Central Coast runs from cool Monterey to Santa Barbara
Santa Barbara's east-west valleys let in cool Pacific air
Paso Robles grows Rhône grapes, Zinfandel and Cabernet
Explain why Pinot Noir suits Oregon
Explain Oregon's labelling and farming culture

Oregon's wine centre is the Willamette Valley, south of Portland, at about 45 degrees north, the same latitude as Burgundy. The climate is cool and maritime, with wet winters and dry summers. David Lett planted Pinot Noir there in 1965, and his 1975 wine did well against Burgundy in a 1979 Paris tasting.

Pinot Noir is over 60% of Oregon's plantings. The cool climate keeps acidity and red fruit, and long, dry autumns ripen it slowly. Volcanic Jory soil in the Dundee Hills and marine sediments in places like Yamhill-Carlton give different styles. Pinot Gris and, increasingly, Chardonnay are the main whites.
Why does Pinot Noir thrive in the Willamette Valley?
A cool climate and long, dry autumns
Cool conditions keep acidity and fruit purity, while dry autumns let grapes ripen slowly.

Oregon wineries are mostly small and family-run. The state requires 90% of a named grape on the label, stricter than federal rules. Sustainable, organic and biodynamic farming are widespread. Burgundian houses like Maison Joseph Drouhin invested from 1987, a sign of respect for the region.
Match each Oregon feature to its detail.
Oregon's history is short but focused.
The Willamette Valley lies at Burgundy's latitude
Pinot Noir is over 60% of plantings
Oregon is mostly small producers, with strict labelling
Explain how ice wine shaped Canada

Washington's vineyards lie east of the Cascade Mountains, which block Pacific rain. The Columbia Valley is a desert, with under 200 mm of rain a year, so all vines are irrigated from rivers. Long summer days at 46 degrees north give ripe fruit with fresh acidity. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling and Chardonnay lead.

Winter can drop below minus 20 degrees, damaging vines. Growers plant on slopes for air drainage and bury canes in some cases. Sandy, wind-blown soils mean phylloxera struggles, so most vines grow on their own roots. Walla Walla, Red Mountain and Yakima Valley are top AVAs.
Which statements about Washington are true?
Most vineyards lie east of the Cascades
Many vines grow on their own roots
Sandy soils keep phylloxera at bay, so own-rooted vines are common.

Canada's main regions are Ontario's Niagara Peninsula, moderated by Lake Ontario, and British Columbia's Okanagan Valley, a dry, warm valley in the interior. Reliable hard winters made Canada the world's leading ice wine producer, especially from Vidal and Riesling. The VQA system sets quality and origin rules.
Which grape is widely used for Canadian ice wine?
Vidal, a hardy hybrid, and Riesling are the main ice wine grapes.
Washington's vineyards are an irrigated desert east of the Cascades
Cold winters and sandy soils mean many own-rooted vines
Canada leads in ice wine from Niagara and the Okanagan
Link each region to its grapes
Match each region to its signature grape.
Each region has found its grape in under a century.
Washington State vineyards rely on irrigation.
Yes. East of the Cascades, rainfall is too low for vines without it.
Which help cool California's coastal vineyards?
California summers are dry. Fog, ocean currents and valley orientation do the cooling.
Prohibition in the United States lasted from 1920 to ____.
1933. Fine wine only really grew again from the 1960s.
AVAs define place; labels need 85% from the area
California's fog and valleys shape its styles
Oregon is Pinot Noir country; Washington an irrigated desert
Canada is the world's leader in ice wine
